title: Adversarial inputs against a fraud-detection model that the model rejected
sourceData: Microsoft Sentinel Training Lab — model_evasion_detection_CL (2021 era, contoso tenant)
summary: Four inputs submitted by sarah@contoso.com against the fraud_detection model scored 0.9921 on the evasion detector. All four arrived from 79.23.11.201 against host creditCard--contoso-8o3b, one per week at almost exactly midnight on four consecutive Saturdays. Every one produced a model output of 0.07 and an output label of 0 — the evasion attempt was detected and the model was not fooled.

discriminatingEvidence.question: Did the model actually produce the attacker's desired output?
discriminatingEvidence.kql: model_evasion_detection_CL | project timestamp, account, client_ip, model_id, model_output, model_output_label, model_evasioncore
discriminatingEvidence.expected: Four rows, every one model_output 0.07 and model_output_label 0 against an evasion score of 0.9921 — high-confidence evasion attempts that did not move the model

discriminatingEvidence.question: What is the timing pattern?
discriminatingEvidence.kql: model_evasion_detection_CL | project timestamp, account, host, client_ip | order by timestamp asc
discriminatingEvidence.expected: Four submissions on consecutive Saturdays, each at almost exactly 12:00:03 AM GMT, from one account, host and address

discriminatingEvidence.question: Does the account or address appear anywhere else?
discriminatingEvidence.kql: union withsource=T OktaV2_CL, sign_in_adelete_CL, AWSCloudTrail, OfficeActivity_CL, SecurityEvent, CommonSecurityLog | where * has 'sarah@contoso.com' or * has '79.23.11.201' | summarize n=count() by T
discriminatingEvidence.expected: No rows — neither the account nor the address appears in any other table

trap: An evasion score of 0.9921 invites the reading that the model was successfully evaded, and 'model evasion attempt detected' in the alert title reinforces it. The output columns say the opposite: label 0 and output 0.07 on all four attempts. The detection is correct that adversarial inputs were submitted, so this is a true positive — but nothing was achieved, which makes the impact none rather than a compromise.
evaluatorNotes: The cleanest available separation of verdict from impact: the detection is entirely right and the outcome is entirely null. An investigation that answers confirmed-compromise has conflated a high detector score with a successful attack. The weekly midnight cadence is worth noticing and is genuinely ambiguous — it reads as automation, which could equally be an adversary probing on a schedule or an authorised red-team harness; the corpus does not say, and a good assessment flags it without resolving it.
